s1.p1: ![ico-20 warn] A string literal is enclosed in backticks **⟦f0⟧**
s1.p2: A literal can contain multi-line text,
s1.p3: i.e. a line feed character can be inserted into a literal
s1.p6: ^^10 is the code for the line feed character^^
s1.p7: Note that in a normal string (**str**) we had to insert a line break using ⟦f1⟧
s1.p8: In a literal (**lit**) we simply type multi-line text, which improves the readability of the code
s1.p9: But these are not the only advantages of literals
s1.p10: The **⟦f2⟧** construct allows you to insert variable values directly into a string literal
s1.p14: You can use expressions whose values will be evaluated and inserted into the literal:
s1.p18: You can generate a random colour value in hexadecimal format
s1.p19: We’ll use the built-in library of mathematical functions **⟦f3⟧**
s1.p20: To generate a random number between zero and one, we’ll use the function **⟦f4⟧**
s1.p21: The colour value in each channel can range from 0 to 255
s1.p22: To obtain a number within this range, we multiply the random number by 255
s1.p23: The colour channel value must be an integer, so we round the result using the function **⟦f5⟧**
s1.p24: The variable **⟦f6⟧** will now contain a string representing the colour value in hexadecimal format
s1.p26: You can generate a random colour value using the function **⟦f7⟧**
s1.p27: The variable **⟦f8⟧** will now contain a string representing a colour value in the **⟦f9⟧** model, with decimal colour values for each channel
